analysis.one_liner: Restructures the consumer financial watchdog and subjects its funding to annual congressional approval.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill on a 32-24 vote, but the full House never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) was created after the 2008 financial crisis to police mortgages, credit cards, and other consumer loans. Unlike nearly every other agency, its money comes automatically from the Federal Reserve, so Congress cannot squeeze its budget year to year. This bill would have cut the CFPB loose from the Fed and forced it into the regular annual appropriations process, where its funding could be reduced or blocked each year. It would also have renamed the agency the "Financial Product Safety Commission" and ended several Federal Reserve-related features of its original setup.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, mortgage lenders, credit card issuers, and other financial companies that are regulated by the CFPB. Moving the agency's funding to the annual appropriations process gives lenders' allies in Congress an annual opportunity to cut the watchdog's budget, since appropriations are where industry pressure is applied most effectively. The rename and the removal of Federal Reserve links are largely cosmetic, but the funding change is the substance.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the mandatory annual transfer of funds to the CFPB from the Federal Reserve and subjects the agency to the regular authorization, budget, and appropriations process of the Treasury Department, meaning its money would depend on annual congressional votes.
Removes the CFPB from within the Federal Reserve System, making it an independent agency.

Renames the agency the "Financial Product Safety Commission" and repeals its authority to locate regional offices in cities with Federal Reserve Banks or branches, along with provisions letting regional Fed bank presidents recommend members of its Consumer Advisory Board.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers who take out mortgages, carry credit cards, or borrow money. A consumer watchdog whose budget can be cut each year by Congress would be far easier to weaken, and weaker enforcement means higher fees, riskier loans, and fewer refunds when companies break the rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill's strongest good-faith argument: the CFPB's automatic, outside-the-appropriations funding is unusual, and putting it through the regular budget process would make the agency answer annually for how it spends public money, adding accountability most agencies face.

The practical cost: funding control is also where regulated industries exert the most pressure on Congress, so annual appropriations would make a consumer regulator permanently vulnerable to being starved of money by the industry it polices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability critique of the CFPB's automatic Fed funding is a real argument that many economists take seriously. But the mechanism this bill used to address it — annual appropriations — is the same channel through which regulated lenders are most able to lobby, so the likely effect would be to make the consumer watchdog weaker rather than merely more accountable. The renaming to "Financial Product Safety Commission" addressed criticism of the agency's name but changed nothing about its power. The bill never became law, so none of these effects took place.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 32-24 and placed it on the House calendar in February 2014, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the two-year Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 18, 2013 by Rep. Randy Neugebauer (R-TX) and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee ordered the bill reported (amended) on a 32-24 vote on November 21, 2013, and formally reported it on February 6, 2014.
The reported bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 257), the list of bills awaiting House floor action.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a vote on the House floor and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, which kept its independent Federal Reserve funding and its enforcement structure unchanged. The banks and lenders that pushed to make the agency's budget vulnerable to annual cuts gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Randy Neugebauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restructure the CFPB and move its funding into the annual appropriations process.

for.name: House Committee on Financial Services
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported (amended) on a 32-24 vote and placed it on the House calendar.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote on the House floor after it was reported to the calendar.

against.name: 24 Financial Services Committee members
against.role: Committee members voting no on reporting the bill
against.what_they_did: Voted against the motion to report the bill (final vote 32-24).

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the bill drew zero cosponsors; the committee advanced it 32-24, and the bill never reached the floor where the broader House would have weighed in.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and mortgage lenders
industries.note: These firms are the CFPB's primary targets. Moving the agency's money from automatic Federal Reserve transfers to annual congressional appropriations would have given their allies in Congress a yearly chance to cut the regulator's budget, weakening enforcement on fees, lending practices, and refunds for consumers.

industries.industry: Payday lenders, debt collectors, and other nonbank consumer finance companies
industries.note: The CFPB also regulates nonbank lenders and collectors that earlier consumer laws largely avoided. A watchdog dependent on annual appropriations would be easier for them to shrink through political channels.
